newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Secret recipe key to success of Belem cakes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Secret recipe key to success of Belem cakes.

text.p: A dozen cream cakes made with a secret recipe sit on a silver tray in a Lisbon shop window.
Fresh cakes have been on display at the blue-tiled Belem Cake shop since the family firm was founded in 1837.
A stone's throw from the presidential palace and the 16th century Jeronimos monastery, the shop draws hundreds of thousands of locals and foreign tourists every year to sample its delights.
"We have succeeded because of our secret recipe -- only four people know it," said Pedro Clarinha, partner and manager of the firm, owned by his family from the start.
"The recipe has never changed. We are faithful to tradition."
Clarinha shares the secret with three cooks, who have shown longstanding loyalty to the firm.
Every day in the factory behind the shop, the cooks shut the door in the Secrets Room and apply their magic.
The result is a concoction of cream, eggs and flour moulded and baked into the Belem Cake that Clarinha says is far superior to any other cream cake made in Portugal.
The factory makes more than three million a year.
"They should be eaten hot and crispy -- with a little cinnamon," Clarinha said.
The Belem Cake Shop took out a patent in 1912 to guard its secret recipe and protect the reputation of a cake that started off as sustenance for hungry monks stepping out of the Jeronimos monastery.
Fans of Belem cakes include Brazilian writer Jorge Amado who has visited the shop several times on trips to Portugal, Clarinha said.
Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso ate the cakes at the presidential palace during a visit in July. The shop often supplies the palace.
Jorge Sampaio stopped at the shop during his campaign to win Portugal's presidency this year. His predecessor Mario Soares was also a devotee.
Sixty percent of the annual cake production is sold at the crowded counter, surrounded by panels of original blue tiles depicting the Belem suburb and displays of quality port wine.
The rest of the cakes are eaten in the coffee shop.
"A lot of people wash down the cakes with a glass of port or Madeira," Clarinha said. "But generally they are eaten between meals."
The Portuguese, the regulars at the Belem cake shop, are renowned for having a sweet tooth.
"The Portuguese love cakes. There are historical reasons: we were one of the first countries to receive sugar cane and refine sugar," Clarinha said.
Outside the shop, some shabby youths -- drug addicts -- hover about in the hope of helping customers to park their cars in return for a few escudos.
"We've called the police to make them go away, but they say they can't do anything because these people are not doing anything illegal," Clarinha said.
"Unfortunately, this problem does scare away some customers. It is a lamentable situation."
The best times for the Belem cake shop are on winter Sunday afternoons when the sun is shining, Clarinha said.
"People want to go out and have a walk, they get hungry and so they stop at the shop for a cake," he said.
The shop does not waste its surplus production at the end of the day. Some is distributed to old people's homes and the rest shared among the staff. A Belem cake must be eaten on the day it is made.
